summary: Djibouti requires nearly every foreign visitor to obtain an eVisa through the official government portal before travel — short-stay eVisas cover up to 14 days and standard ones up to 90 — as visas on arrival are no longer routinely issued.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months on arrival in Djibouti and have at least one blank page for the entry stamp.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (yellow card)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers arriving from countries with a risk of yellow fever transmission — relevant if you arrive overland or via much of sub-Saharan Africa.

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry requirement, but medical facilities are limited and evacuation from remote areas is expensive — comprehensive coverage including medical evacuation is strongly recommended.

onwardTicket.text: The eVisa application asks for a return or onward ticket and proof of accommodation, and airlines check tickets before boarding flights to Djibouti.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; officers may ask visitors to show means of support and accommodation details for their stay.

notes: Khat is legal and widely consumed in Djibouti, but carrying it out of the country can be a serious offense at your next destination.
Do not photograph the port, airport, military installations or foreign bases — Djibouti hosts several and sensitivities are high.

payments.text: Cards are accepted at the bigger hotels and restaurants in Djibouti City, but everywhere else runs on cash. US dollars are widely accepted alongside the Djiboutian franc, and ATMs are essentially confined to the capital.

safety.text: Djibouti City and the main tourist sites are generally safe, with petty theft the main concern. Stay well away from the Eritrean border area and be cautious in remote regions. Carry ID, expect checkpoints, and check current advisories for the wider region before travel.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Djibouti Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to March brings the coolest weather, and the whale shark season in the Gulf of Tadjoura (roughly November to February) plus comfortable conditions for Lake Assal and the Danakil landscapes; summer heat is extreme.

tips.text: From June to August temperatures regularly exceed 45°C. Avoid desert excursions in summer, carry far more water than you think you need, and plan activity for early morning.
Whale sharks gather in the Gulf of Tadjoura roughly from November to February. Book a licensed boat operator in Djibouti City and choose one that enforces no-touch distances.
Arrive with your eVisa approval already printed or saved. Visas on arrival have been largely phased out and airlines check for the eVisa at check-in.
Avoid the border area with Eritrea and be cautious near remote frontier zones — the region carries residual military tension and some unmarked hazards.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Djibouti?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes — Djibouti requires nearly every foreign nationality to obtain an eVisa before travel through the official portal evisa.gouv.dj. A short-stay eVisa covers up to 14 days and a standard one up to 90 days.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Djibouti?
faq.answer: Do not plan on it. Djibouti has shifted visa issuance to the online eVisa system, and airlines generally require the approval before boarding. Apply on evisa.gouv.dj a few days before departure.

faq.question: How much does the Djibouti eVisa cost?
faq.answer: Roughly USD 23 for the short-stay eVisa (up to 14 days) and around USD 93 for the standard eVisa (up to 90 days). The exact amount is shown during the application on the official portal. Confirm there before paying.

faq.question: Can I pay with US dollars in Djibouti?
faq.answer: Yes — US dollars are accepted almost everywhere alongside the Djiboutian franc, and hotels and tour operators often quote prices in dollars. Carry small notes for taxis and markets, where change in dollars can be hard to get.

faq.question: What is worth seeing in Djibouti?
faq.answer: Djibouti packs in Lake Assal (one of the lowest and saltiest lakes on Earth), the lunar landscapes of Lake Abbe, and swimming with whale sharks in the Gulf of Tadjoura in season — most visitors combine all three on short tours from the capital.
